claims.text: During dynamic loading, solute atoms migrate to mobile dislocations.
Migrating solute atoms temporarily pin dislocations through transient solute/dislocation complexes.
Intermittent dislocation pinning produces an intermittent yield point.
Dynamic strain aging enhances strength in dual-phase high-entropy alloys.
Dynamic strain aging contributes to enhanced ductility in dual-phase high-entropy alloys.
AlCoCrFeNi is presented as an example of the relevant dual-phase high-entropy-alloy system.
The proposed initial alloy contains significant chemical heterogeneity, including pre-existing nanoscale solute clusters and precipitates.
Dynamic tests are proposed over strain rates from 10^-3 to 10^0 s^-1.
The proposed experiments extend to temperatures of 500 K.
Solute diffusion is sufficiently active within the proposed temperature range, up to 500 K, to enable solute mobility.
Transient nanoscale solute clusters or precipitates form at the cores of mobile dislocations during dynamic loading.
Relative to an HEA with reduced solute clustering and precipitation, the dual-phase HEA will exhibit an intermittent yield point.
Relative to the baseline, the dual-phase HEA will show strain-rate- and temperature-dependent increases in yield strength.
In-situ high-resolution spectroscopy will reveal transient solute/dislocation complexes during dynamic tests.
Reducing solute clustering and precipitate formation in the baseline alloy will minimize dynamic-strain-aging effects.
The proposed mechanism should operate in chemically heterogeneous dual-phase HEAs between 10^-3 and 10^0 s^-1 and at temperatures up to 500 K.
Dynamic-strain-aging effects will diminish at temperatures too low for significant solute diffusion.
Dynamic-strain-aging effects will diminish in alloys with negligible solute heterogeneity.
Dynamic strain aging is a recognized mechanism in alloy systems other than high-entropy alloys.
The quantitative contribution of dynamic strain aging in high-entropy alloys is not well established, and other deformation mechanisms may contribute.
